q01,single,How long does a controller have to notify a personal data breach to the supervisory authority?,"Without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk; a later notification must state the reasons for the delay.","The controller must notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR
column2: Article 33(1)]. If the notification is not made within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [GDPR

column1: q02,single,On what grounds can a data subject demand the erasure of their personal data?,"Where the data are no longer necessary for their purposes, consent is withdrawn and there is no other legal ground, the data subject objects (Art. 21) with no overriding legitimate grounds, the data were unlawfully processed, erasure is required by a legal obligation, or the data were collected in relation to information society services offered to a child.","A data subject can demand the erasure of their personal data without undue delay where one of the following grounds applies [GDPR
* The personal data are no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed [GDPR
* The data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based (under point (a) of Article 6(1) or point (a) of Article 9(2)) and there is no other legal ground for the processing [GDPR

* The data subject objects to the processing under Article 21(1) and there are no overriding legitimate grounds for the processing, or the data subject objects to the processing for direct marketing under Article 21(2) [GDPR
* The personal data have been unlawfully processed [GDPR
* The personal data have to be erased for compliance with a legal obligation in Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject [GDPR
* The personal data have been collected in relation to the offer of information society services to children referred to in Article 8(1) [GDPR

q03,single,When must a company designate a data protection officer?,"When processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except courts), when its core activities require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, or when its core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data or data on criminal convictions and offences.","A controller and processor must designate a data protection officer in any case where:
* The processing is carried out by a public authority or body, except for courts acting in their judicial capacity [GDPR

* The core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations which, by virtue of their nature, their scope and/or their purposes, require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale [GDPR

* The core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing on a large scale of special categories of data pursuant to Article 9 and personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences referred to in Article 10 [GDPR
In other cases, a controller, processor, or associations and other bodies representing them may—or where required by Union or Member State law shall—designate a data protection officer [GDPR

q04,single,"What is the maximum administrative fine for infringing the basic principles for processing, including the conditions for consent?","Up to EUR 20 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 83(5)).","Infringing the basic principles for processing, including the conditions for consent pursuant to Articles 5, 6, 7, and 9, is subject to administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR, or in the case of an undertaking, up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [GDPR

q05,single,What is the minimum age at which a child can consent to an online service without a parent's authorisation?,"16 years; Member States may provide by law for a lower age, but not below 13 years.","A child can consent directly to information society services (online services) when they are at least 16 years old [GDPR
However, Member States may provide by law for a lower age, provided that it is not below 13 years [GDPR
column2: Article 8(1)]. If a child is below the applicable age, the processing of their personal data is lawful only if and to the extent that parental consent is given or authorised [GDPR

column1: q06,single,"How long does a controller have to respond to a data subject's request to exercise their rights, and can that period be extended?","Without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt; it can be extended by two further months where necessary, and the data subject must be told of the extension within one month.","The controller must provide information on the action taken on a request to exercise data subject rights (under Articles 15 to 22) without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request [GDPR

This period can be extended by two further months where necessary, taking into account the complexity and number of the requests. If an extension is made, the controller must inform the data subject within one month of receipt of the request, together with the reasons for the delay [GDPR

q07,single,Which legal bases make the processing of personal data lawful?,At least one of: consent; necessity for a contract; compliance with a legal obligation; protecting vital interests; a task in the public interest or official authority; or the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party (not for public authorities performing their tasks).,"Processing of personal data is lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the following legal bases applies [GDPR
* **Consent:** The data subject has given consent to the processing of their personal data for one or more specific purposes [GDPR

* **Contract:** Processing is necessary for the performance of a contract to which the data subject is party, or in order to take steps at the request of the data subject prior to entering into a contract [GDPR
* **Legal obligation:** Processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject [GDPR
* **Vital interests:** Processing is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person [GDPR

* **Public interest or official authority:** Processing is necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller [GDPR

* **Legitimate interests:** Processing is necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject which require protection of personal data (this exception does not apply to processing carried out by public authorities in the performance of their tasks) [GDPR

q08,single,Are companies with fewer than 250 employees exempt from keeping records of processing activities?,"In general yes, but not if the processing is likely to result in a risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or data on criminal convictions and offences.","Yes, enterprises or organisations employing fewer than 250 persons are exempt from the obligation to maintain records of processing activities, unless:
* the processing they carry out is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects;
* the processing is not occasional; or
* the processing includes special categories of data (referred to in Article 9(1)) or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences (referred to in Article 10) [GDPR

q09,single,Can a company take decisions about people based solely on automated processing?,"People have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal or similarly significant effects, except where it is necessary for a contract, authorised by law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent; in the contract and consent cases the controller must at least allow human intervention, the person's point of view and a challenge to the decision.","As a general rule, data subjects have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing (including profiling) that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them [GDPR
However, a company can take such decisions if the decision:
* Is necessary for entering into, or the performance of, a contract between the data subject and a data controller [GDPR

* Is authorized by Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject, provided that law lays down suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, freedoms, and legitimate interests [GDPR
* Is based on the data subject's explicit consent [GDPR

When decisions are based on a contract or explicit consent, the controller must implement suitable measures to safeguard the data subject's rights, freedoms, and legitimate interests, which must include at least the right to obtain human intervention on the part of the controller, to express their point of view, and to contest the decision [GDPR
column2: Article 22(3)]. Furthermore, such decisions generally cannot be based on special categories of personal data unless specific exceptions apply along with suitable safeguards [GDPR

column1: q10,single,In which cases is a data protection impact assessment mandatory?,"In particular for a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing (including profiling) that leads to decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, large-scale processing of special categories of data or criminal-conviction data, and systematic large-scale monitoring of a publicly accessible area.","A data protection impact assessment is mandatory prior to processing where a type of processing—particularly using new technologies, and taking into account its nature, scope, context, and purposes—is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR
In particular, it is required in the case of:

* A systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons based on automated processing, including profiling, on which decisions are based that produce legal effects concerning the natural person or similarly significantly affect them [GDPR
* Processing on a large scale of special categories of data (referred to in Article 9(1)) or of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences (referred to in Article 10) [GDPR
* Systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale [GDPR
Additionally, supervisory authorities establish and publish lists of other kinds of processing operations that are subject to the requirement for a data protection impact assessment [GDPR

q11,single,Is real-time remote biometric identification in public spaces by the police allowed under the AI Act?,"It is prohibited unless strictly necessary for one of three objectives: targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and missing persons; preventing a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety or a genuine terrorist threat; or locating or identifying a suspect of an Annex II offence punishable by a custodial sentence of at least four years.","The use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement is generally prohibited, *unless and in so far as* such use is strictly necessary for one of the following specific objectives [AI Act
1. The targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings, or sexual exploitation of human beings, as well as the search for missing persons [AI Act

2. The prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack [AI Act

3. The localisation or identification of a person suspected of having committed a criminal offence for the purpose of conducting a criminal investigation, prosecution, or executing a criminal penalty for specific offences listed in Annex II that carry a maximum custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years [AI Act
Where a Member State decides to allow this use under national law, it must comply with strict conditions and safeguards, including:

* Prior authorization granted by a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority with a binding decision (except in duly justified urgent situations where authorization is requested within 24 hours) [AI Act
* Restriction to confirming the identity of a specifically targeted individual, taking into account the nature of the situation and the consequences for rights and freedoms [AI Act
* Completion of a fundamental rights impact assessment and registration in the EU database (or subsequent registration without undue delay in urgent cases) [AI Act
* Notification to the relevant market surveillance authority and national data protection authority [AI Act

q12,single,What is the maximum fine for a provider that does not meet its obligations for high-risk AI systems under Article 16?,"Up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Art. 99(4)).","Non-compliance with the obligations of providers pursuant to Article 16 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 3 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [AI Act
For SMEs, including start-ups, the fine shall be up to whichever is lower of the aforementioned percentages/amounts or the limits set for SMEs [AI Act

q13,single,Does a chatbot have to tell users that they are talking to an AI system?,"Yes: providers must design AI systems that interact directly with people so that those people are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person; this does not apply to systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences.","Yes. Providers must ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed and developed so that the natural persons are informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant, and circumspect person taking into account the circumstances and context of use [AI Act
column2: Article 50(1)-(2) (part 1/3)]. This obligation does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offences, unless those systems are available for the public to report a criminal offence [AI Act

column1: q14,single,What does the AI Act require about the AI literacy of staff?,"Providers and deployers must take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons operating or using AI systems on their behalf, taking into account their knowledge, experience, education, training and the context of use.","The AI Act requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures, to their best extent, to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [AI Act

When doing so, they must take into account the technical knowledge, experience, education, and training of those persons, the context in which the AI systems are to be used, and the persons or groups of persons on whom the AI systems are to be used [AI Act

q15,single,Which areas of use does Annex III of the AI Act list as high-risk?,"Biometrics; critical infrastructure; education and vocational training; employment, workers' management and access to self-employment; access to essential private and public services and benefits; law enforcement; migration, asylum and border control management; administration of justice and democratic processes.","Annex III of the AI Act lists the following eight areas of use as high-risk:

1. **Biometrics**, in so far as their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law (including remote biometric identification systems, biometric categorisation based on sensitive or protected attributes, and emotion recognition) [AI Act

2. **Critical infrastructure**, specifically safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating, or electricity [AI Act

3. **Education and vocational training** (such as determining access/admission, evaluating learning outcomes, assessing education levels, and monitoring/detecting prohibited student behaviour during tests) [AI Act

4. **Employment, workers’ management and access to self-employment** (including recruitment and selection, decisions affecting terms of work relationships, promotion, termination, task allocation based on individual behaviour/traits, and performance/behaviour monitoring) [AI Act

5. **Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits** (including evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits/services, evaluating creditworthiness/credit scores, life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing, and evaluating/classifying emergency calls and patient triage systems) [AI Act

6. **Law enforcement**, in so far as permitted under relevant Union or national law (including assessing victim crime risks, polygraphs, evaluating evidence reliability, assessing offending/re-offending risks or personality traits, and profiling during criminal detection, investigation, or prosecution) [AI Act

7. **Migration, asylum and border control management**, in so far as permitted under relevant Union or national law (including polygraphs, assessing entry/security/migration/health risks, examining asylum/visa/residence permit applications and evidence reliability, and detecting, recognising, or identifying individuals excluding travel document verification) [AI Act

8. **Administration of justice and democratic processes** (including assisting judicial authorities in researching and interpreting facts/law and applying law in concrete cases or alternative dispute resolution, and influencing election/referendum outcomes or voting behaviour) [AI Act

q16,single,"Above what amount of training computation is a general-purpose AI model presumed to have high-impact capabilities, and therefore systemic risk?",When the cumulative computation used for its training is greater than 10^25 floating point operations (Art. 51(2)).,"A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than $10^{25}$ [AI Act

q17,single,Within how many days must a provider report a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system?,Immediately after establishing a causal link and in any event not later than 15 days after becoming aware of the serious incident; two days for a widespread infringement or a serious and irreversible disruption of the management or operation of critical infrastructure,"A provider must report a serious incident involving a high-risk AI system:
* Not later than **15 days** after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident, made immediately after establishing a causal link or reasonable likelihood of a link [AI Act
* Not later than **two days** after becoming aware of the incident, in the event of a widespread infringement or a serious incident defined under Article 3, point (49)(b) [AI Act
* Not later than **10 days** after becoming aware of the incident, in the event of the death of a person, provided immediately after establishing or suspecting a causal relationship [AI Act

q18,single,Who must deployers of high-risk AI systems assign human oversight to?,"To natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support (Art. 26(2)).","Deployers must assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training, authority, and necessary support [AI Act

q19,single,Which deployers must carry out a fundamental rights impact assessment before using a high-risk AI system?,"Deployers that are bodies governed by public law or private entities providing public services, and deployers of the high-risk systems in points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III (credit scoring, and risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance); critical infrastructure systems (point 2 of Annex III) are excepted.","Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system (referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of those intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III), a fundamental rights impact assessment must be carried out by:
1. Deployers that are **bodies governed by public law** [AI Act
2. Deployers that are **private entities providing public services** [AI Act
3. Deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in **points 5(b) and (c) of Annex III** [AI Act

q20,single,From when are cloud and other data processing service providers no longer allowed to charge customers for switching?,From 12 January 2027 no switching charges may be imposed; between 11 January 2024 and 12 January 2027 only reduced charges that do not exceed the provider's direct switching costs.,"From 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services are no longer allowed to impose any switching charges on the customer for the switching process [Data Act

q21,single,What maximum notice period and transitional period must a data processing service contract provide for switching providers?,"A mandatory maximum transitional period of 30 calendar days to switch (counted after the notice period), and a maximum notice period for initiating the switch that must not exceed two months.","The data processing service contract must provide for:
* **Maximum notice period:** A maximum notice period for the initiation of the switching process that shall not exceed **two months** [Data Act
* **Transitional period:** A mandatory maximum transitional period of **30 calendar days** (initiated after the maximum notice period) [Data Act
column2: Article 25(2)(a)]. If this is technically unfeasible, the provider may indicate an alternative transitional period not exceeding **seven months** [Data Act
column3: Article 25(4)], and the customer also has the right to extend the transitional period **once** for a period it considers more appropriate for its own purposes [Data Act

column1: q22,single,What must connected products be designed to do regarding the data they generate?,"Product data and related service data must by default be easily, securely and free of charge accessible to the user, in a comprehensive, structured, commonly used and machine-readable format and, where relevant and technically feasible, directly accessible.","Connected products must be designed and manufactured in such a manner that product data and related service data (including the relevant metadata necessary to interpret and use those data) are, by default:
* Easily, securely, and free of charge accessible to the user [Data Act
* In a comprehensive, structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format [Data Act
* Directly accessible to the user, where relevant and technically feasible [Data Act

q23,multi,A company suffers a personal data breach that is likely to result in a high risk for the people affected. Whom must it notify and within what time?,"The competent supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware (Art. 33(1)); and the data subjects without undue delay (Art. 34(1)).","The controller must notify:

1. **The supervisory authority:** without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR
2. **The data subject:** without undue delay, when the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR

q24,multi,"A company uses an AI system to score citizens on their social behaviour. Is that allowed, and what is the maximum fine?","Social scoring that leads to detrimental or unjustified treatment is a prohibited practice (Art. 5(1)(c)); non-compliance is subject to fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Art. 99(3)).","The placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system for evaluating or classifying natural persons or groups over a period of time based on their social behaviour or characteristics is prohibited if the resulting social score leads to:
* Detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the contexts where the data was originally generated or collected [AI Act
* Unjustified or disproportionate detrimental or unfavourable treatment in relation to their social behaviour or its gravity [AI Act

Non-compliance with this prohibition is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000, or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7% of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [AI Act
column2: Article 99(3)]. For SMEs (including start-ups), the fine is up to these percentages or amount, whichever is lower [AI Act

column1: q25,multi,"Is an AI system that evaluates students' learning outcomes high-risk, and which provision makes Annex III systems high-risk?","Yes: Annex III, point 3(b) lists AI systems used to evaluate learning outcomes in education, and Art. 6(2) provides that the AI systems referred to in Annex III are considered high-risk.","An AI system intended to be used to evaluate students' learning outcomes (including when those outcomes are used to steer their learning process) in educational and vocational training institutions at all levels is considered high-risk, unless it does not pose a significant risk of harm (such as performing a narrow procedural task) and does not perform profiling [AI Act
Such systems are classified as high-risk under Article 6(2), which establishes that AI systems referred to in Annex III are high-risk [AI Act
column2: Article 6(2)], specifically within **Annex III, point 3(b)** (Education and vocational training) [AI Act

column1: q26,multi,What triggers a data protection impact assessment and what must the controller do if it shows a high risk that cannot be mitigated?,"A type of processing likely to result in a high risk to people's rights and freedoms requires an impact assessment before the processing (Art. 35(1)); if the assessment shows a high risk without mitigating measures, the controller must consult the supervisory authority before processing (Art. 36(1)).","A data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is triggered prior to processing when a type of processing—particularly using new technologies and taking into account its nature, scope, context, and purposes—is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [GDPR
Specifically, a DPIA is required in cases of:

* A systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects relating to natural persons based on automated processing (including profiling) on which decisions are based that produce legal effects or similarly significantly affect the natural person [GDPR
* Processing on a large scale of special categories of data (under Article 9(1)) or of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences (under Article 10) [GDPR
* Systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale [GDPR
* Additionally, supervisory authorities establish, make public, and communicate lists of other kinds of processing operations that require a DPIA [GDPR

If a DPIA indicates that the processing would result in a high risk in the absence of measures taken by the controller to mitigate the risk, the controller must consult the supervisory authority prior to processing [GDPR
column2: Article 36(1)]. When consulting, the controller must provide the supervisory authority with specified information including their respective responsibilities (and those of processors), processing purposes and means, safeguards, DPO contact details, and the DPIA itself [GDPR

column1: q27,multi,Can an AI provider process special categories of personal data to detect bias in a high-risk AI system?,"The GDPR prohibits processing special categories of data in general (Art. 9(1)), but the AI Act lets providers of high-risk systems exceptionally process them where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to safeguards and conditions, e.g. bias detection cannot be done with other data, there are technical limits on re-use and state-of-the-art security measures (Art. 10(5)).","Yes, providers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process special categories of personal data to the extent that it is strictly necessary for ensuring bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards for fundamental rights and freedoms and specific conditions [AI Act
The processing must meet all of the following conditions:
- The bias detection and correction cannot be effectively fulfilled by processing other data, including synthetic or anonymised data [AI Act
- The data are subject to technical limitations on re-use and state-of-the-art security and privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation [AI Act

- Measures are in place to ensure the data are secured, protected, and subject to suitable safeguards, including strict access controls and documentation to avoid misuse and ensure only authorised persons with appropriate confidentiality obligations have access [AI Act
- The data are not transmitted, transferred, or otherwise accessed by other parties [AI Act
- The data are deleted once the bias has been corrected or the personal data has reached the end of its retention period, whichever comes first [AI Act

- Records of processing activities under Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 or Directive (EU) 2016/680 include the reasons why processing special categories of personal data was strictly necessary to detect and correct biases and why that objective could not be achieved using other data [AI Act

q28,multi,What rights does a person have to challenge or understand a decision taken about them with a high-risk AI system?,"Under GDPR Art. 22 they have the right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, and in the contract and consent cases the right to human intervention, to express their view and to contest the decision; under AI Act Art. 86 an affected person has the right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the AI system's role in the decision and the main elements of the decision.","An affected person subject to a decision taken by a deployer based on the output of certain high-risk AI systems (specifically those listed in Annex III, with the exception of point 2 systems) has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken, provided the decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them in a way they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety, or fundamental rights [AI Act

This right to an explanation applies only to the extent that the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law, and it does not apply where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [AI Act

q29,multi,How does the user's right to access data under the Data Act relate to the GDPR right to data portability?,"The Data Act is without prejudice to personal data protection law, and where users are data subjects the rights in its Chapter II complement the access and portability rights under GDPR Arts. 15 and 20 (Data Act Art. 1(5)); in a conflict the data protection law prevails; the GDPR right (Art. 20) lets a person receive the data they provided in a structured, machine-readable format and transmit it to another controller.","Insofar as users are data subjects, the rights laid down in Chapter II of the Data Act complement the GDPR rights of access by data subjects and to data portability under Articles 15 and 20 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 [Data Act
Additionally:
* The Data Act applies without prejudice to EU and national law on the protection of personal data, and in the event of a conflict, EU data protection and privacy law prevails [Data Act

* Any failure to agree on arrangements for transmitting data between a data holder and a third party must not hinder, prevent, or interfere with a data subject's rights under the GDPR, particularly the right to data portability under Article 20 [Data Act

q30,multi,Which has the higher maximum fine: using a practice prohibited by the AI Act or infringing the GDPR principles for processing?,"The AI Act: up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices (Art. 99(3)), against up to EUR 20 000 000 or 4 % for infringing the GDPR basic principles (Art. 83(5)).","Using a practice prohibited by the AI Act has the higher maximum fine.
Specifically:

* **AI Act prohibited practices** (non-compliance with Article 5) are subject to administrative fines of up to **EUR 35 000 000** or, for an undertaking, up to **7 %** of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [AI Act

* **GDPR processing principles** (infringements of the basic principles for processing pursuant to Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9) are subject to administrative fines of up to **EUR 20 000 000** or, in the case of an undertaking, up to **4 %** of its total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [GDPR
